title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
summary: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

title: Beyond Direct Binding: Serotonin Rewires Model Brain Plasma Membrane-Mediated Communication Pathways in Y4R
summary: Serotonin, an endogenous neurotransmitter, modulates pancreatic polypeptide (PP) recognition by the neuropeptide Y4 receptor (Y4R), a mechanism relevant to altered serotonergic signaling associated with metabolic disorder and anxiety. Although recent experiment demonstrates serotonin modulated PP dissociation kinetics of Y4R through membrane allostery, the molecular mechanism of serotonin induced lipidomic reorganization of the brain plasma membrane (BPM) relevant for Y4R activation is unknown. To this end, a total of 825.9 ns long all atom molecular dynamics simulations at 310 K elucidate the concentration-dependent coupling between serotonin partitioning, selective lipid reorganization, and PP binding and Y4R activation relevant intra-receptor communication in a heterogeneous, asymmetric model BPM. In the absence of serotonin, Y4R preferentially associates with the anionic lipids. Serotonin preferentially localizes at the lipid water interface over the PP binding and activation-associated regions of Y4R. At 6 mM, serotonin preferentially contacts phosphocholine species depleted from Y4R, whereas at 50 mM, phosphatidylinositol 4,5 bisphosphate dominates both microenvironments. These changes align with the selective remodeling of lipid networks, enhanced lipid chain ordering, and modest bilayer compaction. Weighted implementation of suboptimal paths analysis reveals concentration-dependent reorganization of communication pathways between experimentally implicated PP binding and activation associated Y4R residues. Collectively, these findings connects serotonin dependent selective lipid redistribution to altered intramolecular communication between Y4R residues associated with PP binding and G-protein coupling, and provide a framework for future experiments investigating membrane-mediated neuromodulation and neuronal signaling. These findings provide a basis for exploring lipid-targeted pharmacology as a complementary strategy to modulate GPCR allostery by altering membrane composition rather than directly targeting the receptor.

title: Simulating Bead-Tethered Biomolecules: Force-Probe Coupled Steered Molecular Dynamics (fp-SMD) in Optical Tweezers Force Spectroscopy
summary: Interpreting single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) data from optical tweezers with steered molecular dynamics (SMD) is hindered by a severe timescale mismatch: SMD trajectories span nanoseconds to microseconds, while SMFS experiments unfold over milliseconds to seconds, forcing SMD to pull six to nine orders of magnitude faster than experiment and systematically distorting rupture forces, molecular pathways, and kinetic intermediates. We introduce force-probe coupled steered molecular dynamics (fp-SMD), which explicitly propagates the force probe (the optically trapped bead) alongside the biomolecule within a single classical Hamiltonian description of the coupled molecule-linker-bead system. A Predict-Correct Trajectory Propagation (PCTP) scheme resolves the resulting computational bottleneck by alternating a bead-propagation step, with the molecular center of mass (COM) held fixed, and a molecular step in which metadynamics and transition-state theory identify the kinetically resolved intermediate reached at each macroscopic time step. On the cholesterol--{beta}-cyclodextrin ({beta}-CD) host-guest complex, fp-SMD reproduces the experimental rupture-force histogram directly at matched conditions, without extrapolation from standard SMD. fp-SMD further resolves how applied force reshapes the molecular escape pathway: we find that cholesterol dissociates via a high-angle route at low force and a direct, small-angle route at high force--providing, to our knowledge, the first direct structural evidence for force-induced pathway switching in a small host-guest system, a mechanism believed to underlie catch-slip bond behavior.

title: Nuclear speckles comprise hierarchical nanoscale interaction networks that shape molecular dynamics
summary: Biomolecular condensates organize essential cellular processes, but how their internal architecture regulates molecular behavior in living cells remains poorly understood. Here, we use MINFLUX nanoscopy for quantitative single-molecule imaging and live-cell tracking to resolve the organization and dynamics of specific macromolecules within nuclear speckles. Rather than behaving as uniform liquid-like compartments, nuclear speckles are hierarchically organized into dynamic nanoscale interaction networks. Proteins and RNAs assemble into molecular clusters that generate transient interaction nanodomains, where individual molecules alternate between diffusion and confinement while exploring higher-order networks. Physiological and genetic perturbations selectively remodel molecular clustering and nanodomain organization, and these changes are not consistently coupled to changes in the abundance of the measured components. Together, these findings reveal a multiscale organization of nuclear speckles in which molecular clustering, transient confinement, and dynamic exchange represent distinct but interconnected features of condensate architecture in living cells.

title: Kinetics and Evolution-guided Design of High Fidelity CRISPR-Cas Endonucleases
summary: Finding high-fidelity CRISPR-Cas variants is critical for both the precision of in vitro DNA detection and the safety of in vivo gene-editing therapeutics. However, the large size of the Cas enzymes and the distinct selection criteria between its natural evolution and clinical practice lead to extensive experimental trials and limited success rate for de novo design, directed evolution and protein language model (PLM)-based filtering. Here, we present a physics-driven, PLM-assisted approach that utilizes atomistic molecular dynamics simulations and automated path searching to efficiently obtain the atom-level kinetic insights, including the transition state structures, for the conformational changes of R-loop formation that dictate the off-target DNA recognition and cleavage by Cas. We show that these kinetic insights can pinpoint the fidelity-diminishing protein residues during the early stage of target recognition. Integrated with PLM-filtering of the mutants on these sites, this approach identified high-fidelity SpyCas9 and FnCas12a variants (4.49-fold and 6.69-fold increase respectively from wild-type), surpassing previously reported counterparts at minimal cost of only a few wet-lab validations (cellular genome-editing and ribonucleoprotein cleavage assays respectively).

title: Lac1-dependent ceramide synthesis couples septum assembly to cell separation in Schizosaccharomyces pombe
summary: Ceramides are precursors of complex sphingolipids and bioactive membrane lipids. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, they are produced by a ceramide synthase with two catalytic subunits, Lac1 and Lag1, which are redundant but not functionally equivalent: only Lac1 is required for normal growth and cell size. Why Lac1 has this unique role, and how ceramide synthesis contributes to cell morphogenesis, remain unknown. Here, we show that Lac1 couples septum assembly to cell separation. Cells lacking Lac1 die predominantly during cell separation and build septa with a thinner primary layer and markedly thicker secondary layers, accompanied by altered deposition of {beta}-(1,3)-glucans and galactomannan. These defects are not rescued by osmotic stabilization. The essential glucan synthase Bgs4 is mislocalized to cytoplasmic granules, and total {beta}-(1,3)-glucan synthase activity is partially reduced. Nevertheless, Ags1, Bgs1 and Bgs4 accumulate to higher levels and persist almost twice as long at the division site, indicating defective clearance rather than delivery of the septum-synthesis machinery. Plasma membrane sterol distribution remains unaffected. To accurately impair ceramide synthesis, we isolated thermosensitive lac1-ts alleles in a lag1{Delta} background. Their substitutions cluster in the conserved TRAM/LAG1 domain. Metabolic labeling showed that these alleles reduce ceramide synthesis at the restrictive temperature. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that two substitutions perturb distinct contacts with C26-CoA, while Lac1-M167T loses its endoplasmic reticulum localization. Acute inactivation recapitulates the deletion phenotype, causing septum accumulation and cell death. Together, our findings establish that Lac1-dependent ceramide synthesis is required for the orderly completion of septum assembly and cell separation.

title: Patient-specific metabolic fluxes reflect molecular subtype and heterogeneity in breast cancer
summary: Tumor metabolism is dynamic and context-dependent, yet gene expression provides only an indirect view of metabolic activity. We combined patient-specific genome-scale metabolic models with supervised and unsupervised machine learning to infer metabolic fluxes for 1,223 TCGA breast tumor and normal samples under a uniform physiological medium. Flux profiles distinguished tumor from normal tissue under patient-grouped nested cross-validation (ROC-AUC up to 0.989) and predicted receptor status and molecular subtype (e.g., Basal-like versus other tumors, AUC = 0.966), but not stage, nodal status or age. Within tumors, metabolic variation was continuous rather than organized into discrete groups and aligned only partially with clinical classifications. These findings support a view of breast cancer metabolism as a structured but continuous landscape that reflects molecular subtype and receptor status, and provide a reproducible framework to characterize tumor heterogeneity.

title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
summary: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, cause a range of symptoms, and cause significant global yield loss in fruit and vegetable plants. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, Tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, CGMMV and ToMMV, at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively. The structures reveal divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. While ToMMV is genetically similar to the canonical Tobamovirus TMV and displays a structure closely resembling TMV, CGMMV employs a more hydrophobic packing strategy, particularly in the solvent-exposed inner loop region of the coat protein. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, this study reports a newly identified electrostatic patch existing at the lower alpha-helix region of the coat protein that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, with host family-specific amino acid substitutions among Tobamoviruses. Our study elucidates the structural mechanics and evolutionary strategies driving virion stability and host diversity while maintaining a conserved helical assembly. These findings reveal how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent packing strategies drive viral stability and host adaptation within a strictly conserved quaternary scaffold.

title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
summary: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
summary: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

title: Molecular insights into the regulation of coenzyme selection in NADP-specific glutamate dehydrogenase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae
summary: Coenzyme specificity is one of the crucial aspects of the functional regulations in enzymes. Understanding the molecular basis of coenzyme specificity in glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is highly essential as this is the only enzyme that fulfils various physiological demands in terms of energy production and/or nitrogen assimilation via its strict functional regulation by connecting carbon and nitrogen metabolic cycles in every living organism. We have studied S. cerevisiae GDH3 (ScGDH3), as a model system for NADP-specific fungal GDHs. K272R and S250E mutants of ScGDH3 exhibited remarkable alteration in coenzyme specificity, with 15-55-fold and 3-14-fold more preference towards non-specific coenzymes [NAD(H)], respectively. S250E exhibited higher NADH affinity (~ 1.3-fold) than that of towards NADPH. K272R showed ~ 10-fold increased coenzyme affinity (1/KM) and binding affinity (1/kd) towards NADH, compared to the wild type enzyme (ScGDH3-WT). We solved the crystal structure of ScGDH3-K272R complexed with NADP+ at 2.50 [A] resolution with a unique oligomeric arrangement having two distinct subunit conformations (''open'' and ''super-closed'') and it is the first structure of a GDH from S. cerevisiae. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide insights into NADH binding and its increased affinity to ScGDH3-K272R. Further structure-based sequence analyses unravelled that a lysine and an arginine are naturally preferred residues for providing NADP(H) and NAD(H) specificity, respectively for various amino acid dehydrogenases. Taken together biochemical and structural data, our study successfully illustrates the evolutionary conserved mechanism of coenzyme related regulation in fungal and other GDHs; as well as amino acid dehydrogenases.

title: AI-Guided Structure-Aware Modeling and Thermal Proteomics Reveal Direct Demethylzeylasteral-ACLY Interaction
summary: Identifying the direct molecular targets of bioactive natural products remains a central challenge in chemical biology. Here we present an integrated experimental-computational framework, that combines matrix-augmented thermal proteomics with HoloGNN, a holistic graph neural network, to systematically prioritize and validate protein-ligand interactions. Benchmarking with PDBbind datasets HoloGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance. Applying this framework to 50 structurally diverse natural products identified Demethylzeylasteral as a direct interactor of ACLY. Orthogonal biochemical assays confirmed micromolar binding and enzymatic inhibition. In an imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like mouse model, Demethylzeylasteral reduced disease severity and inflammatory cytokine expression. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed that Demethylzeylasteral reverses keratinocyte hyperproliferation and suppresses ACLY-dependent lipid metabolic reprogramming. Together, this scalable, closed-loop strategy integrates thermal proteomics and machine learning to uncover direct targets of natural products and provides mechanistic evidence linking ACLY inhibition to therapeutic modulation of inflammatory pathology.

title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
summary: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators (R1-R5). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1, R2, R3, and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1-R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

title: GNG2-MRAS interaction regulates SHOC2-dependent RAF activation and MAPK signaling
summary: Dysregulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway is a hallmark of many human cancers and RASopathies. The SHOC2-MRAS-PP1C; (SMP) holophosphatase complex is a crucial regulatory node of this pathway. It activates the MAPK pathway by dephosphorylating the inhibitory phosphoserine on RAF kinases and thereby relieving RAF autoinhibition. Although GNG2, the {gamma}-subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins, has recently emerged as a negative modulator of MAPK signaling, its molecular mechanism of action remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify GNG2 and its truncated variants as inhibitors of SMP complex assembly by directly targeting MRAS. Using NanoBiT live-cell bioluminescence, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), biolayer interferometry (BLI), and molecular dynamics simulation studies, we demonstrate that full-length GNG2 (residues 1-71aa) and two helical fragments ({Delta}1, residues 1-29aa and {Delta}2, residues 30-71aa) bind MRAS, disrupt SMP complex formation, and therefore prevent RAF dephosphorylation. Expression of the truncated GNG2 variants significantly reduced phosphorylation of ERK in cells, consistent with inhibition of pathway activation. Furthermore, a short peptide synthesized from the GNG2 {Delta}2 sequence effectively disrupted SMP complex formation in both purified protein systems and live cells and potently attenuated MAPK signaling. Molecular dynamics simulation studies revealed that GNG2 variants engage with the Switch I/II regions of MRAS, sterically interfering with SHOC2-PP1C association. Together, these findings establish GNG2 as a direct regulator of SMP complex assembly and demonstrate that GNG2-derived peptides represent a promising strategy for disrupting SHOC2-MRAS interactions and suppressing MAPK signaling in RAS/RAF-driven pathologies.
